title: Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence
covers: How labeled antibodies are used to locate a protein in tissue: antibody types, the three staining methods, fluorescence microscopy, the laboratory protocol and its pitfalls.

items.p: Immunohistochemistry finds a specific protein where it sits, in fixed tissue or cells, using an antibody that carries a visible label.
It tells you which protein, where, when, and whether two proteins sit together (co-localization).

ul: Clinic: typing cancers by their molecular markers; identifying cell types (CD4, CD7)
Research: presence, distribution, subcellular location and changes of a protein
Specificity: a binding site reacts with one determinant
Cross-reactivity: it reacts with more than one
Affinity: the strength of one site binding one determinant

items.p: Direct: the labeled antibody binds the antigen itself.
Indirect: an unlabeled primary antibody (say, from rabbit) binds the antigen. A labeled secondary antibody against rabbit antibodies then binds the primary.

table: Amplifies weak signals; tolerates small antigen changes
Highly specific; low background; reproducible; unlimited supply

ul: Immunoenzymological: enzyme label (horseradish peroxidase, alkaline phosphatase), often with biotin-streptavidin; colored precipitate or emitted light
Immunoelectron microscopy: electron-dense label (ferritin, colloidal gold) seen as black dots

items.p: A fluorochrome absorbs light at one wavelength and emits at a longer one (lower energy).
The microscope has two filters. The first lets through only the exciting light. The second blocks it and lets through only the emitted light.

ul: DAPI: DNA dye, blue under UV
GFP: a fluorescent protein, not a dye
Photobleaching (fading): use less light for less time, more fluorophore, or sturdier fluorophores
Fix (formaldehyde), dehydrate (alcohol), clear (xylene), embed (paraffin), cut 1–10 μm sections, mount
Antigen retrieval: heat or protease uncovers the epitopes
Block endogenous biotin and enzymes, and non-specific sites
Primary antibody, then labeled secondary antibody, then detection
Strong background: endogenous biotin or enzymes, cross-reacting antibodies
Weak staining: poor enzyme activity or weak primary antibody
Autofluorescence: from the tissue or the fixation

items.p: Always run a positive and a negative control. Related antibody techniques are flow cytometry, Western blotting and ELISA.

cards.a: A specific antigen in situ, in fixed tissue or cells, using a labeled antibody
Direct: labeled antibody binds the antigen. Indirect: unlabeled primary antibody, then a labeled secondary antibody against the primary's species.
One determinant only; more than one determinant; strength of a single site–determinant bond
Amplify weak signals and tolerate antigen variation; more false positives and batch-to-batch variability
Highly specific, low background, reproducible, unlimited supply; may not work across species
Absorbs light at one wavelength and emits at a longer wavelength

cards.q: Roles of the two filters in a fluorescence microscope
cards.a: First: passes only exciting light. Second: blocks it and passes only emitted light.
DAPI: blue DNA dye excited by UV. GFP: a green fluorescent protein, not a dye.
Less intense or shorter illumination, more fluorophore, more robust fluorophores
Horseradish peroxidase and alkaline phosphatase (with biotin-streptavidin)
Ferritin or colloidal gold; seen as small black dots
Fixation, dehydration, clearing (xylene), paraffin embedding, sectioning, mounting
Heat or protease treatment that makes epitopes available to the antibody

cards.q: Common causes of high background in IHC
cards.a: Endogenous biotin or enzymes, and cross-reacting antibodies (fix with blocking and antibody dilution)

questions.stem: What is immunohistochemistry?

options.A: In-situ detection of a specific antigen in fixed tissue with an antibody
options.B: Detection of a specific antigen in a tissue lysate after gel electrophoresis
options.C: Detection of a soluble antigen in serum in a coated microplate
options.D: Counting of labeled cells in suspension passing a laser
options.E: Detection of a nucleic acid sequence in fixed tissue with a probe

questions.explanation: IHC is the in-situ detection of a specific antigen/protein in fixed tissue sections and cells using an antibody, visualized with a microscope. B: That is Western blotting. C: That is ELISA. D: That is flow cytometry. E: IHC detects antigen with antibody.

questions.stem: What did Albert Coons achieve in 1941?

options.A: Produced the first monoclonal antibody from a single clone
options.B: Described the hinge and Fc regions of immunoglobulin G
options.C: Localized mycobacterial antigens with an enzyme-labeled antibody
options.D: Localized pneumococcal antigens with a FITC-labeled antibody
options.E: Developed the electron microscope for colloidal gold labels

questions.explanation: Coons (1941) localized pneumococcal antigens in infected tissues using a fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-labeled antibody. A: Not what is attributed to Coons. B: Not what is attributed to Coons. C: The antigen was pneumococcal and the label fluorescent. E: Not what is attributed to Coons.

questions.stem: Which label is matched with the microscopy or detection used?

options.A: Fluorescent dyes: electron microscopy
options.B: Electron-dense particles: electron microscopy
options.C: Horseradish peroxidase: fluorescence microscopy
options.D: Electron-dense particles: fluorescence microscopy
options.E: Alkaline phosphatase: electron microscopy

questions.explanation: Antibodies are labeled with fluorescent dyes (fluorescence microscopy), electron-dense particles (electron microscopy), enzymes (horseradish peroxidase, alkaline phosphatase) or radioactive elements. A: Fluorescent dyes need fluorescence microscopy. C: It is an enzyme label. D: They are seen by electron microscopy. E: It is an enzyme label.

questions.stem: An antibody combining site reacts with more than one antigenic determinant. Which term applies?

options.A: Specificity
options.B: Affinity
options.C: Cross-reactivity
options.D: Avidity
options.E: Co-localization

questions.explanation: Cross-reactivity: an antibody combining site reacts with more than one antigenic determinant. Specificity: with only one. A: Specificity is reaction with only one determinant. B: Affinity is the strength of a single site–determinant reaction. D: Not the term defined here. E: A feature of protein distribution.

questions.stem: Specificity is the ability of a combining site to react with only one determinant. How is antibody affinity defined?

options.A: Ability of one combining site to react with one determinant
options.B: Total binding strength of an antibody's combined sites
options.C: Ability of an antibody population to react with several antigens
options.D: Number of epitopes recognized by an antiserum
options.E: Strength of reaction between one determinant and one site

questions.explanation: Affinity is the strength of the reaction between a single antigenic determinant and a single combining site on the antibody. Specificity is the ability to react with only one determinant. A: That is specificity. B: That is avidity. C: That is cross-reactivity. D: Not the definition.

questions.stem: Which questions can an IHC experiment answer about a protein?

options.A: Where and when it is expressed; co-localization
options.B: Its full amino acid sequence and exact molecular weight
options.C: Its gene copy number and mutations
options.D: Its concentration in serum over time
options.E: Its three-dimensional crystal structure

questions.explanation: IHC shows who is the target, where it is expressed (localized expression), when (time-specific) and co-localization, in fixed tissue or cells. B: Not provided by IHC. C: Not provided by IHC. D: IHC works on fixed tissue. E: Not provided by IHC.

questions.stem: Why is IHC used in clinical histopathology?

options.A: To measure plasma protein concentration
options.B: To sequence tumor DNA for mutations
options.C: To type cancers from molecular markers
options.D: To culture tumor cells for drug testing
options.E: To count circulating tumor cells in blood

questions.explanation: Clinical use: diagnosis of abnormal cells, such as specific cancer types based on molecular markers (breast, lung, prostate) and cell-type biomarkers (CD4, CD7). Research use: presence, tissue distribution, subcellular localization, expression changes, co-localization. A: Not an IHC use. B: Not an IHC use. D: Not an IHC use. E: That would be flow cytometry.

questions.stem: In indirect IHC of a human tissue with a rabbit primary antibody, what is the secondary antibody?

options.A: A marker-coupled antibody directed against the human antigen
options.B: An unlabeled antibody directed against human antibodies
options.C: A marker-coupled rabbit antibody against a second epitope
options.D: A marker-coupled antibody directed against rabbit antibodies
options.E: A marker-coupled antibody directed against mouse antibodies

questions.explanation: Direct IHC: a marker-coupled antibody binds the antigen. Indirect IHC: a primary antibody (e.g. rabbit) binds the antigen and marker-coupled secondary antibodies directed against rabbit antibodies bind the primary. A: That would be direct IHC. B: The secondary carries the marker and targets the primary's species. C: The secondary recognizes the rabbit antibody. E: It must match the species of the primary.

questions.stem: How do polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies differ?

options.A: Polyclonal: one clone, different epitopes; monoclonal: several clones, a single epitope
options.B: Polyclonal: several clones, different epitopes; monoclonal: one clone, a single epitope
options.C: Polyclonal: several clones, a single epitope; monoclonal: one clone, different epitopes
options.D: Polyclonal: from mice; monoclonal: from rabbits
options.E: Polyclonal: labeled; monoclonal: unlabeled

questions.explanation: Polyclonal: a mixture of antibodies of different affinity, made by different clones, recognizing different epitopes. Monoclonal: identical copies of one antibody made by the same clone, recognizing a single epitope. A: The clone numbers are swapped. C: The epitope numbers are swapped. D: Species does not define the type. E: Labeling does not define the type.

questions.stem: A researcher needs to detect a protein expressed at a very low level whose sequence varies slightly between individuals. Which antibody type suits best, and what is its drawback?

options.A: Monoclonal; batch-to-batch variability and more false positives
options.B: Polyclonal; limited tolerance of antigen polymorphism
options.C: Monoclonal; low specificity with high background
options.D: Polyclonal; inability to amplify weak signals
options.E: Polyclonal; batch-to-batch variability and more false positives

questions.explanation: Polyclonal antibodies amplify signal from low-expression targets, tolerate minor antigen changes (polymorphism) and detect robustly, but give more false positives from cross-reaction and vary from batch to batch. A: Those drawbacks belong to polyclonal antibodies. B: Polyclonals tolerate minor antigen changes. C: Monoclonals are highly specific with less background. D: Polyclonals amplify signal from low-expression targets.

questions.stem: Each of the following is an advantage of monoclonal antibodies EXCEPT:

options.A: Detection across a range of species
options.B: Less background staining
options.C: Highly reproducible results
options.D: Unlimited supply
options.E: Less cross-reactivity with other proteins

questions.explanation: Monoclonals: highly specific, less background, less cross-reactivity, homogeneous and reproducible, unlimited supply; but so specific that they are less likely to detect across a range of species. B: Listed advantage. C: Listed advantage. D: Listed advantage. E: Listed advantage.

questions.stem: Which are the three immunohistochemical staining methods of the lecture?

options.A: Immunofluorescence, flow cytometry, Western blotting
options.B: Immunoenzymological staining, ELISA, immunoelectron microscopy
options.C: Immunofluorescence, hematoxylin-eosin, immunoelectron microscopy
options.D: Direct, indirect and sandwich staining
options.E: Immunofluorescence, immunoenzymological, immunoelectron

questions.explanation: Immunohistochemical staining: immunofluorescence, immunoenzymological staining and immunoelectron microscopy. A: The last two are other immunostaining techniques. B: ELISA is another technique. C: Hematoxylin-eosin is not an immunostain. D: These are not the three methods listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about fluorochromes is correct?

options.A: They absorb light at one wavelength and emit at a shorter wavelength
options.B: They emit light without needing excitation
options.C: They absorb electrons and appear as black dots
options.D: They absorb light at one wavelength and emit at a longer wavelength
options.E: They convert a substrate into a colored precipitate

questions.explanation: Fluorochromes absorb light at one wavelength and emit light at a longer wavelength (fluorescence); the emitted photon is necessarily of lower energy than the absorbed one. A: The emitted photon has lower energy, so longer wavelength. B: Excitation is required. C: That describes electron-dense labels. E: That describes enzyme labels.

questions.stem: Which statement about DAPI and GFP is correct?

options.A: DAPI is a fluorescent protein; GFP is a DNA dye that fluoresces green
options.B: DAPI is a blue DNA dye; GFP is a fluorescent protein
options.C: DAPI labels antibodies red; GFP labels DNA blue
options.D: DAPI is an enzyme label; GFP is an electron-dense label
options.E: DAPI absorbs red light and fluoresces green; GFP absorbs UV

questions.explanation: GFP is a green fluorescent protein, not a dye. DAPI is a general fluorescent DNA dye that absorbs UV light and fluoresces bright blue. Cy3, Cy5 and Alexa dyes were developed for fluorescence microscopy. A: Reversed. C: DAPI is a blue DNA dye. D: Neither. E: DAPI absorbs UV and fluoresces blue.

questions.stem: In a fluorescence microscope, what does the second filter do?

options.A: Passes the exciting light and blocks the emitted wavelengths
options.B: Passes just the wavelengths that excite the dye
options.C: Blocks the exciting light and passes the emitted wavelengths
options.D: Focuses electrons on the specimen
options.E: Blocks ultraviolet and infrared light equally

questions.explanation: Two sets of filters: the first passes only the wavelengths that excite the dye; the second blocks this light and passes only the wavelengths emitted when the dye fluoresces. A: Reversed. B: That is the first filter. D: Not a fluorescence microscope function. E: Not its described role.

questions.stem: In the composite micrograph of a mitotic cell, which structures are shown by which probes?

options.A: Microtubules red, centromeres green, DNA blue with DAPI
options.B: Microtubules green, centromeres red, DNA blue with DAPI
options.C: Microtubules blue with DAPI, centromeres red, DNA green
options.D: Microtubules green, centromeres blue with DAPI, DNA red
options.E: Microtubules green with GFP, centromeres red, DNA unstained

questions.explanation: Spindle microtubules: green fluorescent antibody; centromeres: red fluorescent antibody; DNA of the condensed chromosomes: blue dye DAPI. A: The antibody colors are swapped. C: DAPI stains DNA. D: DAPI stains DNA. E: DNA is stained blue with DAPI.

questions.stem: A fluorescent signal fades while the slide is being examined. Which measure does NOT reduce this problem?

options.A: Lengthening the time of light exposure
options.B: Reducing the intensity of light exposure
options.C: Increasing the concentration of fluorophores
options.D: Using more robust fluorophores
options.E: Shortening the time of light exposure

questions.explanation: Photobleaching solutions: reduce the intensity or time-span of light exposure, increase the concentration of fluorophores, use more robust fluorophores less prone to bleaching. B: A listed solution. C: A listed solution. D: A listed solution. E: A listed solution.

questions.stem: Which elements belong to immunoenzymological staining?

options.A: FITC or Cy3, two filter sets, fluorescent detection
options.B: Ferritin or colloidal gold, electron beam, black dots
options.C: HRP or alkaline phosphatase, DAPI, ultraviolet detection
options.D: Radioactive iodine, biotin-streptavidin, autoradiography
options.E: HRP or alkaline phosphatase with biotin-streptavidin

questions.explanation: Enzymes: horseradish peroxidase, alkaline phosphatase; biotin-streptavidin amplification; detection is colorimetric (violet precipitate) or chemiluminescent (light emission at 425 nm). A: That is immunofluorescence. B: That is immunoelectron microscopy. C: DAPI is a fluorescent DNA dye. D: Not the method described.

questions.stem: In immunoelectron microscopy, which labels are used and how do they appear?

options.A: Ferritin or colloidal gold; bright green spots
options.B: FITC or DAPI; small black dots
options.C: Ferritin or colloidal gold; small black dots
options.D: HRP or alkaline phosphatase; violet precipitate
options.E: Biotin or streptavidin; light at 425 nm

questions.explanation: An electron-dense label (ferritin, colloidal gold) is conjugated to the Fc portion of a specific antibody (direct) or to an anti-immunoglobulin reagent (indirect); it absorbs electrons and appears as small black dots. A: Electron-dense labels appear as black dots. B: These are fluorescent labels. D: That is enzyme staining. E: That is chemiluminescent detection.

questions.stem: Put the steps of sample preparation in order: (1) paraffin embedding, (2) fixation with formaldehyde, (3) clearing with xylene, (4) dehydration with alcohol, (5) sectioning with a microtome.
questions.explanation: Fixation (formaldehyde), dehydration (alcohol), removal of ethanol with an organic solvent (xylene), embedding (paraffin), sectioning (microtome), mounting on slides. A: Dehydration with alcohol precedes xylene, which removes the ethanol. B: Fixation comes first. C: Xylene comes before embedding. E: Embedding precedes sectioning.

questions.stem: What is antigen retrieval?

options.A: Heating or protease treatment to make epitopes available
options.B: Blocking endogenous biotin and enzymes before the primary antibody
options.C: Incubation with buffer to cover nonspecific reactive sites
options.D: Removal of ethanol with an organic solvent
options.E: Rapid freezing of tissue to preserve antigens

questions.explanation: Antigen retrieval: heating or treatment with protease to make the epitopes available for antibody binding. B: A separate blocking step. C: That is blocking. D: That is clearing with xylene. E: An alternative to embedding.

questions.stem: What must be blocked before adding the primary antibody, and why is careful sample preparation critical?

options.A: Endogenous antibodies and complement; to keep cells alive
options.B: Exogenous fluorochromes; to prevent photobleaching
options.C: Endogenous DNA and RNA; to keep nuclei unstained
options.D: Endogenous biotin and enzymes; to keep antigenicity
options.E: Secondary antibody sites; to amplify the signal

questions.explanation: Endogenous biotin and endogenous enzymes (peroxidases, alkaline phosphatase) are blocked before the primary antibody. Preparation must maintain cell morphology, tissue architecture and antigenicity of target epitopes. A: Tissue is fixed, and the items blocked are biotin and enzymes. B: Not the blocking step described. C: Not the blocking step described. E: Not the blocking step described.

questions.stem: Which statement about tissue sectioning is correct?

options.A: Sections are 1–10 mm thick, cut from fresh unfixed tissue
options.B: Sections are 100–500 μm thick, cut after embedding in agar
options.C: Sections are 1–10 μm thick, cut after embedding in resin or wax
options.D: Sections are 1–10 nm thick, cut with a laser
options.E: Sections are 1–10 μm thick, cut before fixation with glutaraldehyde

questions.explanation: Tissue is fixed (formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde), embedded in a supporting medium (resins or waxes, hardened by cooling or polymerization) or rapidly frozen, and cut into sections 1–10 μm thick with a microtome. A: Sections are micrometres thick and the tissue is fixed and supported. B: Not the thickness or medium given. D: Not what is described. E: Fixation comes first.

questions.stem: An IHC slide shows staining everywhere, masking the target. Which steps reduce this background?

options.A: Antigen retrieval, concentrating antibodies, longer incubation
options.B: Blocking buffer, diluting antibodies, changing incubation
options.C: Omitting the secondary antibody and adding more substrate
options.D: Stronger fixation and thicker sections
options.E: More intense light and more fluorophore

questions.explanation: Non-specific binding causes high background. Reduce it by incubation with a buffer that blocks reactive sites, dilution of primary or secondary antibodies, and changing the time or temperature of incubation. A: Concentrating antibody and longer incubation increase background. C: Not the measures listed. D: Not the measures listed. E: Those concern photobleaching.

questions.stem: Which pairing of IHC problem and cause is correct?

options.A: Autofluorescence: poor enzyme activity
options.B: Weak target staining: endogenous biotin
options.C: Strong background: low primary antibody potency
options.D: Weak target staining: antibody cross-reactivity
options.E: Autofluorescence: tissue nature or fixation method

questions.explanation: Strong background: endogenous biotin or reporter enzymes, or antibody cross-reactivity. Weak target staining: poor enzyme activity or primary antibody potency. Autofluorescence: nature of the tissue or fixation method. Get the right control. A: That causes weak target staining. B: That causes strong background. C: That causes weak staining. D: That causes background.

questions.stem: Which techniques are listed as other applications of the immunostaining concept, and what should each experiment include?

options.A: Flow cytometry, PCR and karyotyping; positive and negative controls
options.B: Flow cytometry, Western blotting and ELISA; positive and negative controls
options.C: Western blotting, Southern blotting and ELISA; a positive control
options.D: ELISA, mass spectrometry and flow cytometry; no controls if monoclonal
options.E: Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy; a negative control

questions.explanation: Other techniques: flow cytometry, Western blotting, ELISA. Variables: tissue type, fixation, pre-treatment, antibody selection; use appropriate positive and negative controls. A: PCR and karyotyping are not immunostaining techniques. C: Southern blotting detects DNA, and both controls are needed. D: Controls are required. E: These are IHC staining methods.
